query: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW is a single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy with excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but very poor room-temperature ductility, while its irradiation resistance has primarily been proposed by first-principles calculations. What intervention could improve its room-temperature ductility without compromising its high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline under room-temperature, 1600 °C, and irradiation assessments, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor alloying addition of vanadium (≈1–2 at.%) into equal-atomic NbMoTaW will improve its room-temperature ductility by promoting more active dislocation motion and more favorable grain boundary characteristics, without compromising its high-temperature mechanical strength (at 1600 °C) or its irradiation resistance as predicted by first-principles calculations.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW single-phase BCC refractory high-entropy alloy
generation.intervention: Microalloying via the addition of 1–2 at.% vanadium during alloy synthesis (e.g., vacuum arc melting) to produce a modified NbMoTaW–V alloy
generation.conditions: Synthesis under high-purity argon/ vacuum conditions to ensure a single-phase BCC structure; room-temperature tensile tests, 1600 °C high-temperature compression tests, and ion irradiation assessments (with dose levels comparable to prior theoretical conditions) for performance evaluation
generation.structural_mediator: Vanadium is expected to segregate at grain boundaries and slightly refine the grain structure, facilitating enhanced dislocation mobility at low temperatures while preserving the overall BCC lattice stability
generation.mechanism: The addition of V reduces local barriers to dislocation motion (by modifying grain boundary chemistry and possibly lowering the stacking-fault energy) to improve ductility at room temperature. At high temperatures, the dominant refractory element interactions preserve the BCC phase stability required for superior mechanical performance, and the irradiation resistance remains largely governed by the inherent defect recombination properties confirmed by prior calculations
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the untreated NbMoTaW baseline (which shows very poor room-temperature ductility), the V-alloyed variant is expected to exhibit a measurable increase in room-temperature ductility (e.g., increased strain-to-failure) while retaining comparable high-temperature strength (at 1600 °C) and irradiation resistance
generation.baseline: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW with its single-phase BCC microstructure, excellent high-temperature performance, and irradiation resistance as predicted by first-principles calculations, but with very poor ductility at room temperature
generation.boundary: The vanadium content must remain within 1–2 at.% to avoid the formation of secondary phases that could detrimentally affect high-temperature strength or irradiation behavior; processing conditions must ensure complete solid solution and retention of the single-phase BCC structure
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism of grain boundary modification and dislocation mobility enhancement is anticipated from analogous alloy systems, the exact quantitative improvement in ductility and potential subtle impacts on high-temperature oxidation behaviors or irradiation-induced defect evolution require experimental validation

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a series of NbMoTaW alloys with 0, 1, and 2 at.% vanadium additions using standardized vacuum arc melting. Characterize phase purity (using X-ray diffraction and electron microscopy) and measure room-temperature tensile properties, 1600 °C compression properties, and perform ion irradiation tests. Use atom probe tomography (APT) or TEM to confirm vanadium segregation at grain boundaries.
measurements: 1600 °C compressive yield strength and stress-strain behavior
Irradiation-induced defect density and microstructural evaluation via TEM/APT
Phase analysis via XRD to confirm retention of the single-phase BCC structure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the vanadium-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility without a measurable decrease (>5–10%) in high-temperature mechanical performance or irradiation resistance compared to the control NbMoTaW, the hypothesis should be rejected.
